ROBERTSO¶ *Department of Pediatrics and *Departments of Medicine and of Biochemistry and Biophysics, The Howard Hughes Medical Institute Laboratories and The Metabolic Research Unit, University of California, San Francisco, California 94143; and lCenter for Reproductive Sciences, Department of Biochemistry, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons, New York, New York 10032 Communicated by Rudi Schmid, June 23, 1980 The biosynthesis of human corticotropin ABSTRACT (ACIH) was studied in organ culture of pituitary adenomas and by translating mRNA from an ectopic ACTHproducing tumor in a cellfree system.

Peptides similar to human ACTH,,-lipotropin, and the aminoterminal glycopeptide are cleaved from a common precursor with an apparent molecular weight of 35,000 on sodium dodecyl sulfate/polyacrylamide gels.
The precursors synthesized in pituitary and ectopic ACIHproducing tissues are indistinguishable.
The cleavage sites of the peptide chain appear to be similar to those previously deduced for murine and bovine ACTH.
Immunoprecipitation studies suggest that the primary structure of the precursor peptide is Simi in all three species.

However, glycosylation is different in the human and murine precursors: the precursor to human ACTH appears to be glycosylated only in the aminoterminal fragment, not in the ACTH or, Blipotropin sequences.
Studies with an autopsied normal human pituitary suggest that neither normal nor adenomatous pituitary tissue glycosylates the ACTH sequence.
In several animal species, corticotropin (ACTH), f3lipotropin (/3LPH), endorphin, and melanotropin (MSH, melanocytestimulating hormone) arise from a common precursor protein (proACTH/LPH) (19).

In the cultured mouse pituitary tumor line AtT20, a precursor protein of apparent Mr 30,000 is cleaved at two places to yield ACTH, f3LPH, and a large aminoter- minal fragment lacking known biological function (14).

In certain tissues, further cleavage of ACTH yields aMSH and corticotropinlike intermediate lobe peptide; theBLPH sequence may be cleaved to yield various peptides, including 'yLPH, f3MSH, and, 3endorphin.
The precursor protein and its major cleavage products other than f3LPH may be glycosylated in various ways prior to cleavage (10, 11).

In the intermediate lobe of bovine pituitary, ACTH, , BLPH, and an aminoterminal region of t105 amino acids arise from a common precursor protein whose sequence was deduced from the mRNA nucleotide sequence (8, 9).
Less information exists about the genesis and processing of human ACTH, but it suggests a similar scheme.
Plasma concentrations of immunoassayable pituitary ACTH and f3LPH increase and decrease concomitantly in normal and pathologic states (1214).
Immunoassayable f,-LPH and endorphin are found along with ACTH in pancreatic (15) and pulmonary (16) tumors causing the ectopic ACTH syndrome.

It is not known if pituitary and ectopic ACTH arise from the same precursor synthesized from the same gene.

In order to elucidate the pathways of processing of human proACTH/LPH, we studied an ectopic ACTHproducing tumor by immunoprecipitation and tryptic mapping of proACTH/LPH coded by tumor mRNA in a cellfree proteinsynthesizing system.
We also studied the incorporation of [a5S]methionine and [3H]glucosamine in organ culture of human pituitary tumors and measured ACTH in peptides extracted from a human pituitary post-mortem.
Our data indicate that human ACTH arises from a precursor of apparent Mr 35,000 which appears to be the same in pituitary and ectopic ACTHproducing tumors.
This precursor is cleaved by a proteolytic process indistinguishable from that seen in AtT20 cells.
However, unlike in AtT20 cells, only the aminoterminal fragment of the human precursor is significantly glycosylated.
MATERIALS AND METHODS RNA Preparation and Translation.
Metastatic tissue from an ectopic ACTHproducing carcinoma of the pancreas from a 10year-old boy was frozen in liquid nitrogen at surgery and stored at -70°C until used.
Frozen tissue was pulverized and dissolved in 5 M guanidine thiocyanate/50 mM TrisHCl, pH 7.5/10
mM, EDTA!/5% (wt/vol) 2mercaptoethanol/1% sodium lauroyl sarcosinate containing 0.45 g of CsCl per ml for preparation of RNA by centrifugation through a cushion of 5.7 M CsCl (18).
Polyadenylylated RNA [poly(A)-RNA] was selected from the total RNA by chromatography on oligo(dT)-cellulose (19).
The poly(A)-RNA was translated in a cellfree rabbit reticulocyte system treated with micrococcal nuclease to destroy endogenous mRNA (20).
Immunoprecipitations.
Immunoprecipitations from the cellfree translation products were performed by modifications of the method of Kessler (21) as described (1, 22).
All antibodies were raised in rabbits by E. Herbert, except for the antiLPH, provided by C. H. Li.

Antibody against ACTH-(124) was purified by affinity chromatography against aACTH-(124) bound to Sepharose 4B (3), and antibody against endorphin was raised against purified conjugated endorphin; neither antibody contained material that crossreacted with other regions of the ACTH/LPH precursor (unpublished observations).
AntiLPH crossreacted with /3endorphin (23).

In Vitro Tissue Labeling.
A 1mg sample of pituitary adenoma from a 12year-old girl with Nelson syndrome

[ACTHproducing tumor of the pituitary after bilateral adrenalectomy in a patient with Cushing disease (24)] was obtained at surgery and incubated for 2.5 hr at 370C in 100 p1 of Dulbecco's minimal essential medium deficient in methionine and cysteine and supplemented with 80, Ci of [a`SImethionine (New England Nuclear; 1075 Ci/mmol; 1 Ci = 3.7 X 1010 becquerels).

For carbohydrate labeling, a sample of tumor from a 19year-old man with Cushing disease was incubated for 6 hr in the same medium deficient in glucose and supplemented with 1.0 mCi of [3H]glucosamine (New England Nuclear; 20 Ci/mmol).
After incubation, the tissues were washed in phosphatebuffered saline free of calcium and magnesium and lysed in 50 gl- of isoelectric focusing lysis buffer (25).
Gel Electrophoresis and Tryptic Peptide Analysis.
Onedimensional electrophoresis was performed in NaDodSO4 gels containing 12.5% (wt/vol) polyacrylamide as described by Laemmli (26).

For twodimensional electrophoresis of total cell proteins, the first dimension consisted of nonequilibrium pH gradient gel electrophoresis with pH 3.510 Ampholines for 1600 Vhr, and the second dimension consisted of NaDodSO4 gel electrophoresis in 12.5% polyacrylamide (27).

Portions of dried gels were rehydrated in 0.1 M NH4HCO3 after autoradiography, and immunoprecipitates or peptides labeled in vivo were eluted by digestion with tosylphenylalanyl chloromethyl ketonetreated trypsin (25, ug/ml) for 18 hr at 370C (28).
Tryptic peptides were analyzed by paper electrophoresis at pH 6.5 as described (1, 4).
Normal Pituitary ACaTH Profile.
A pituitary from a patient who died from bronchopneumonia was obtained 3 hr after death.

After the tissue was extracted with 5 M acetic acid, the acidsoluble proteins were electrophoresed on a 12% acrylamide/NaDodSO4 tube gel, protein was eluted from gel slices, and ACTH was measured by radioimmunoassay with antibody against ACTH-(124) (10).

The data also show that this hproACTH/LPH appears to be processed according to the same general outline that has been elucidated for murine AtT20 cells wherein two proteolytic events occur separating the precursor into (3LPH, ACTH, and an aminoterminal glycopeptide (10, 30).
It is not clear from these studies whether f3LPH is processed further to yield f3endorphin, an event that occurs more slowly than the first two proteolytic events (10, 30).

Because the same peptide cleavage pattern appears to occur in mice and humans and because the murine and bovine sequences are known to contain lysine and arginine residues at the cleavage points (9, 30) it is likely that similar tryptic sites exist in the human precursor.
Although the pattern of proteolytic cleavage of the human and murine precursors is similar, the pattern of glycosylation is not.

In both AtT20 cells (29) and rat pituitaries (ref. 6 and unpublished data) two major forms of the proACTH/LPH molecule exist, each containing carbohydrate attached to the amino terminus; one also contains a carbohydrate side chain in the ACTH-(139) region of the precursor This difference in the two forms of rodent proACTH/LPH is also seen in its end products, where glycosylated (Mr 13,000) and nonglycosylated (Mr 4500)
ACTH appear in approximately equal proportions.
However, Fig. 2 shows there is only one major form of proACTH/LPH and only one detectable form of ACTH-(139) labeled in the human pituitary adenoma.

The radioimmunoassay profile of the postmortem normal human pituitary ACTH is consistent with this interpretation of Fig. 2; there is essentially no ACTH immunoactivity between Mrs 9000 and 15,000i.e., the size expected for glycosylated ACTH-(139) in this gel system (10, 11).
No substantial amounts of glycosylated ACTH have been observed in autopsied and biopsied human pituitary tissue (31).
Thus, glycosylation of human proACTH/LPH appears to occur only in the aminoterminal fragment, creating a heterogeneity of Mr and pI in the precursor.

This glycosylation explains the array of "satellite spots" seen on the autoradiograph on the acidic side of the hproACTH/LPH spot; this array is also seen at Mr - 22,000 (pH 6.0), the putative ACTH/aminoterminal intermediate, and at Mr z 18,000 (pH 5.0), the putative aminoterminal fragment.
The human and murine proACTH/LPH molecules are similar antigenically as well as being similar in their general processing.

Antisera directed against murine ACTH-(124), f3LPH, and endorphin immunoprecipitate the human peptides, suggesting considerable amino acid homology between the two species in the carboxyterminal half of the precursor molecule.

However, two different antisera, BFT and Bgt, directed against the aminoterminal region of murine proACTH/LPH of Mr 29,00032,000 failed to precipitate the hproACTH/LPH, suggesting that there may be different antigenic determinants in the aminoterminal regions of the murine and human precursors.

Although unlikely, it is possible that all the antibody reacting with the aminoterminal region in these preparations is directed against a portion of the aminoterminal glycopeptide such as the ", yMSH" region (9) that is immunologically similar in f,-LPH and oaACTH and that the excess f,-LPH or ACTH (which contain MSH regions) in both assays may have competed for the antibody, thus preventing immunoprecipitation of the hproACTH/LPH.

Tryptic mapping of the murine proACTH/LPH by the same procedures yields a similar pattern; however, one less tryptic peptide is observed (1, 2, 10).
Human f3LPH contains two tryptic peptides labeled with methionine, f3LPH-(4751) and flLPH-(6169), which are unresolved as a single peak with RLrS 0.05 (Figs. 3 and 4 A and B).
By contrast, mouse and rat flLPH contain only one methioninelabeled tryptic peptide, 13LPH-(6169) (2, 32).
Like all other mammalian ACTHs of known sequence, human ACTH contains only one methionine-labeled tryptic peptide, aACTH-(18), represented by a peak with RLy, 0.19 (Figs. 3 and 4 A and C).
In Fig.

4A, the peak of f3LPH peptides at RLys 0.05 contains 720 cpm and the ACTH peak at RLys 0.19 contains 340 cpm, a ratio of 2.1, in agreement with the assignment of two and one methionine residues to f3LPH and ACTH, respectively.
The two peaks at RLys 0.4 and 0.6 are similar to those observed in the AtT20 system, where they were shown to derive from the aminoter- minal region of proACTH/LPH (2).
The absence of this material in ACTH (Fig. 4C) and flLPH (Fig. 4B) also suggests that this activity derives from the amino terminus.

Furthermore, this region contains 350 cpm, suggesting that it represents variable cleavage of a peptide containing a single methionine residue; the aminoterminal fragment of bovine proACTH/ LPH, the only species for which sequence data exist, contains a single methionine (9).
The origin of the material migrating in the acidic region (RLYS < 0) in Figs. 3 and 4A is unknown.

Thus, analysis of the electrophoretic pattern of tryptic fragments from hproACTH/LPH shows that this material contains the ACTH and f3LPH sequences and further suggests that the human and murine precursors are similar.
These data suggest that proteolytic processing of the peptide backbone of the human ACTH precursor in these tumors is similar to that observed in the mouse and rat.
Preferred tryptic cleavages appear to occur at certain loci, yielding the active fragments of the precursor molecule.
Thus, the pattern of ACTH processing elucidated from mouse AtT20 cells may be a general mammalian feature.
